content: The Jerusalem cherry (Solanum pseudocapsicum) is a plant that belongs to the Solanaceae family, the same botanical family as the deadly nightshade. The fruit of this plant is toxic and should not be consumed. While it is often cultivated as an ornamental houseplant, in certain regions of Australia, it has become an invasive weed. This plant is a perennial species that thrives in USDA hardiness zones up to zone 8. It is native to Peru and has the ability to withstand frosts and cold temperatures. The typical lifespan of the Jerusalem cherry is approximately 10 years. It begins producing fruit in its second or third year of growth and continues to bear fruit annually thereafter. The fruit of Solanum pseudocapsicum closely resembles cherry tomatoes in both taste and texture, which can lead to confusion. However, unlike cherry tomatoes, the fruit of the Jerusalem cherry contains a toxic compound known as solanocapsine. This alkaloid is chemically related to other toxic substances found in the Solanaceae family, such as solanine and atropine. Although the toxin present in the fruit is harmful, it is not typically life-threatening. Ingestion of the fruit may result in gastrointestinal symptoms, including vomiting and gastroenteritis.
